fields.AN_Notes: General_Guidance strategy verbatim: 'Writing clear and detailed prompts to generate relevant and personalised content for youth.' and 'Training youth workers to divide information clearly and into defined blocks - prompts - will make it easier for AI systems to understand and process their input.' (4.2.4.4 National Focus Group - Portugal, Q4 and Q5). Prompting is a competence to be trained (Learning_Content) and a recommended practice. AN_Population: the codebook has no value for general youth work. The report addresses youth work professionals in non-formal education without any focus on homelessness or precarious living conditions, so Homelessness_Youth is not supported; youth work is coded as part of child and youth services (Child_Family_Welfare) together with Education_Professional for the professional AI-literacy setting (resolved by the AI Agent Review, vocabulary gap flagged for domain experts). Bias axis: only the language barrier from the work's own focus groups (AI tools primarily in English, Greek-speaking youth and youth workers disadvantaged, 4.2.4.3 Q3 and 4.2.5) is coded as Language_Culture; gender and age differences come from a reported survey (3.2) without a bias analysis and are not coded as axes. Harm: English as default language of AI tools limits usability for non-English-speaking youth workers and young people (Exclusionary_Norms, own focus-group result, boundary case). Mitigation: training and critical evaluation of AI output to avoid biases are proposed as competences of youth workers, no evaluation. Gender understanding follows the male/female comparison of section 3.2, taken up in the conclusions, without a definition (Implicit_Only, Binary_Categorical). Bias understanding is recognisable only as bias inherited from training data (Implicit_Only). Competence frameworks (DigComp, ETS model, Hofstede's dimensions) frame neither gender nor bias, so no theory reference. Studientyp Empirisch because the focus groups with youth work professionals are the work's own data; the report also contains a desk review of competence frameworks.

fields.AN_Notes: Other_Axis: marital or relationship status and household composition, analysed through the 'Really Single' model and the broad cohabitation definition. Gender is coded from the own survey with women's shelters on digital exclusion. Religion appears only as a co-mentioned proxy ground and is not coded. Intersectional is not coded, since intersectional discrimination is named in background and recommendations without a result that depends on a combination of axes. Harm types: Direct_Discrimination through citizenship and foreign-affiliation inputs of the 'Model Abroad', Indirect_Discrimination through apparently neutral household, residency and income inputs acting as proxies and through digital-only access, Exclusionary_Norms through dominant-group norms of household and family embedded in the models and the digital-only default. Stereotyping of foreigners as fraud-prone is argued as a political narrative rather than a system output and is left uncoded. No group-level quality difference could be measured because demographic data was denied, so Disparate_Performance is not coded. Mitigation: proposed ban on citizenship and foreign-affiliation inputs (Pre_Processing) and proposed caseworker training, impact assessments, audits, transparency, independent oversight and non-digital access (Organisational_Process). UDK's equalisation of true positive rates is reported and criticised, not presented as an evaluated mitigation. Gender is treated through women in crisis centres without a definition or recognisable understanding; the glossary enumeration of sex, gender identity and intersex status is a legal list that the analysis does not follow. Theory references: structural discrimination and othering frame the treatment of bias.

fields.AN_Notes: Systematic review of nine implementation studies of predictive risk tools in child welfare, structured by CFIR and the ethical evaluation frameworks of Russell (2015) and Drake et al. (2020). AN_Mitigation_Status Evaluated is a synthesised evaluation, not the review's own experiment: the review reports that the post-processing fairness correction of Purdy and Glass (2023), group-specific risk thresholds, reduced false positive and false negative error rates among four subgroups; it also reports the racial equity report of Putnam-Hornstein et al. (2022) finding comparable accuracy across racial and ethnic groups. Other mitigation stages remain description or recommendation: exclusion of bias-prone variables after community consultation and feature selection (Pre_Processing), stakeholder consensus, training against automation bias and external ethics reviews (Organisational_Process). Race_Ethnicity is the axis of the synthesised subgroup analyses, thresholds and equity reports; gender is mentioned once as a subgroup dimension of accuracy checks and socioeconomic status only in a cited discussion sentence, so both stay uncoded. Harm types follow the review's own synthesis: subgroup error rates and equity in subgroups as Disparate_Performance, historical bias in administrative records and racial disparities in screening outcomes as Indirect_Discrimination. AN_Bias_Definition Explicit rests on the adopted equity criterion of Russell (2015), 'equity evaluates whether predictions function consistently across subgroups'. AN_Theory_Reference No (resolved by the AI Agent Review): Russell (2015) and Drake et al. (2020) are evaluation criteria and a practical framework that the review uses as an assessment checklist, and CFIR is an implementation framework; the review itself names the limited use of theoretical frameworks as a gap and mentions feminist and other critical theories only as a future-research suggestion. Boundary case flagged for domain experts.

AI_Literacies.snippet: These strategies can enhance algorithm literacy and support social workers in correctly interpreting the output of the model, thus making informed decisions.
